items.case: Appeals against inclusion before West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals (court-47)
items.headline: In 7k WB booths, all cleared voters face EC exclusion plea
items.claim: In 7,335 polling booths across 23 districts of West Bengal, every elector whom judicial officers examined and found eligible in the adjudication of logical discrepancies faces an appeal against inclusion before the SIR appellate tribunals, the Hindustan Times reported on 11 November from a report on the tribunals by the Civic Research Group, which it describes as a research collective based in Kolkata. The paper reports that these booths held 27,277 such electors, that by the group's analysis the appeals against 21,615 of them, 79%, were pending and those against 5,662 had been disposed of, and that every one of the state's 294 constituencies has at least one such booth. It reports from the group's report that the share of cleared electors facing an appeal is highest in Kalimpong at 71.4%, Purba Bardhaman at 59.7% and Darjeeling at 59.3%, and lowest in Dakshin Dinajpur at 39.3%, Cooch Behar at 39.4% and Nadia at 39.5%. The group compiled its statewide figures from the tribunals' appeal portal, the paper reports, and its published count is 16,08,175 appeals against inclusion, 15,26,933 of them pending and 81,242 disposed of. The group says the portal does not show the outcome of a disposed appeal.
items.quote: These 7,335 booths held 27,277 voters who judicial officers cleared. Of these, 21,615 (79%) were pending and 5,662 were disposed of, according to the CRG analysis.
items.response: The Commission declined to comment, the paper reported. A senior official of the Commission told it, on condition of anonymity, that the appeals were filed by officials of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer who had the authority to do so as per the Supreme Court, that this was a technicality, that an appeal against an elector does not mean the elector was ineligible to vote, and that the electors' names appeared in the supplementary lists, which meant they were eligible to vote in the Assembly election. The Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October cited a letter from the Chief Electoral Officer's office saying the office's officers had filed the appeals as authorities under the Representation of the People Act (court-57).

items.case: Letters of the Chief Electoral Officer's office, West Bengal, to the Registrar General of the Calcutta High Court on adjudication cases that judicial officers had not decided or not e-signed (court-59)
items.headline: Election Commission Says Around 6,000 Voters in Bengal Are Still ‘Under Adjudication’. In Just 22 Seats, the Real Number is Almost 30,000
items.claim: The office of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer told the Registrar General of the Calcutta High Court in memos dated 12 October and 29 October 2026 that judicial officers had not decided 815 adjudication cases and had decided 5,004 more without e-signing them, The Wire reported on 13 November. The two figures add to 5,819, which is the 'around 6,000' of The Wire's headline. The Wire publishes the memo of 12 October, No. 9806-Home (Elec) from the Additional Chief Electoral Officer. It says the Commission's IT team wrote on 6 August that the logins of the judicial officers of the constituencies concerned had been reactivated, and it asks the Registrar General to have those officers e-sign the decided cases and decide the rest at the earliest. It refers to an earlier memo of 7 August. The Wire reports that the memo of 29 October gives the same two figures, and that the office asked district election officers the same day to report on these cases by 3 November, before the integrated draft roll of the special summary revision due on 23 November. The Wire says the Commission's ECINET report 'Individuals Under Adjudication' of 9 April, which it has seen, records 22,163 cases that judges had not decided when the judicial review ended and 83,504 that they had decided and not signed, 44,027 of them found eligible. It reports that 12,337 of the undecided cases were in Murshidabad, 5,194 in Purba Bardhaman and 3,374 in South 24 Parganas, across 67 constituencies, with 3,183 in Farakka. The Wire's own count, from the rolls of 304 polling stations in 11 of Murshidabad's 22 constituencies as revised up to 6 April, is 29,347 electors still marked under adjudication, which it says is five times the number the Chief Electoral Officer's office gives for the whole state. In three polling stations of Mahadebnagar gram panchayat in Farakka it counts 1,914, and booth level officers told it that the judicial review there never took place. The Wire says an elector whose case was never decided has no order to take to the appellate tribunals and was not able to vote in April.
items.quote: In memos dated October 12 and 29, the office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), West Bengal, told the Calcutta high court that across the entire state of Bengal, 815 cases had still not been decided by judicial officers.
items.response: The Wire says it asked the Chief Electoral Officer on 5 November why 22,163 cases had not been decided by the time the roll was frozen, when and by whom they were decided while the judicial officers' logins were inactive, and how many of those electors were found eligible, and that it will update the report on a reply. It gives no response from the Chief Electoral Officer's office, the Election Commission or the High Court.

items.case: W.P.(C) No. 1246 of 2026, the petition on the Commission's functioning (court-52, court-53), in which LiveLaw reports the affidavit was filed, and the petition on Delhi's revision, W.P.(C) No. 1188 of 2026 (court-54, court-60, court-61), with which The Hindu reports it, Supreme Court
items.headline: ‘Alive’ to voters’ need to find their names on the electoral roll, ECI assures Supreme Court
items.claim: The Election Commission filed a supplementary affidavit in the Supreme Court on 14 November 2026, The Hindu reported. LiveLaw reports that Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu filed it on behalf of the Commission in the writ petition that leads the batch on the Commission's functioning, W.P.(C) No. 1246 of 2026 (court-52, court-53). The interrogatories that INDIA bloc leaders asked the Court on 16 November for leave to serve also describe it as sworn by Yeturu (court-78). The Indian Express describes it as a joint affidavit of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and the Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi. The Hindu gives no case number and reports the affidavit together with the concerns about Form 6 raised by the petitioners in the case on Delhi's revision, in which Anjali Bhardwaj is a petitioner (court-54, court-60, court-61). The affidavit says the Commission took note of the Court's suggestion at the hearing of 28 October that it reach out to electors left off as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, and that by a communication of 6 November it directed the Chief Electoral Officers of the states and union territories where the revision is under way, which LiveLaw lists as Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland, to let electors left off the draft roll submit the enumeration form (Annexure A) to the Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer for their current ordinary residence. An elector who has not shifted may submit the signed form with an Annexure B statement giving the reason it was not submitted earlier, in person or through family members, to the Electoral Registration Officer, the Assistant Electoral Registration Officer or the booth level officer, and that an option to submit it online with e-sign will be available on ECINET. An elector who has shifted within the state does not need Form 8 and may submit the enumeration form with an Annexure C statement giving the new address and Assembly constituency, and proof of address, to the Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer of the new constituency. The affidavit says booth-wise lists of electors marked absent, shifted, dead or duplicate are to be displayed afresh with the probable reasons why they were not included, and that Electoral Registration Officers are to process the enumeration forms of these electors under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 and re-assign the same EPIC number to them. It says a previously enrolled elector who has already filed Form 6 need not submit the enumeration form again, and that such applications will be processed under the clarification of 3 November (court-60). It repeats that clarification, that no prosecution will be launched against anyone for filing Form 6 merely because the applicant was enrolled before the revision and was not in the draft roll, provided the applicant is not enrolled in any other Parliamentary or Assembly constituency and the declaration is otherwise in accordance with law. ThePrint, carrying a PTI report, also reported the affidavit and says the Chief Electoral Officers have been asked to give the clarification wide publicity, in local languages as well. The affidavit says a mechanism has been directed to ensure that no eligible elector is deprived of the chance to be included in the final roll, with due care to avoid duplicate enrolment. It also says that after a new Deputy Election Commissioner joined on 2 November, a work order of 4 November gave oversight of the Commission's IT division to a Senior Deputy Election Commissioner, that the Director General (IT) puts the division's files to the Commission through that officer, and that the IT division has always been under the supervision of a Deputy Election Commissioner. The Times of India also reported the affidavit, from PTI. The batch on the Commission's functioning was tentatively listed for 17 November (court-53), and the Delhi case is listed for 19 November (court-61).
items.quote: Electors who have not shifted may submit the signed Enumeration Form (Annexure A) with the Annexure-B statement giving the reason for the earlier non-submission of the Enumeration Form.
items.response: The affidavit is the Commission's own account of what it has done since the hearing of 28 October (court-54). The Indian Express and ThePrint quote it as saying it 'remains committed to its constitutional duty of ensuring the purity of the election process' and that problems 'have been and will be' arising from time to time. None of the five reports gives a response from the petitioners or a hearing on the affidavit.

items.case: Appeals by the Election Commission before West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals against electors cleared by judicial officers (court-47, court-57, court-58)
items.headline: 'Who Ordered 16 Lakh Appeals Against Voters Cleared by Judges?' Jawhar Sircar Asks West Bengal CEO
items.claim: Jawhar Sircar, a retired IAS officer, former Rajya Sabha member and former Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal, wrote to the state's Chief Electoral Officer, Neelam Meena, on 13 November 2026 asking who ordered the appeals filed before the appellate tribunals against 16,10,311 electors whom judicial officers had found eligible, and on what authority, The Wire reported on 14 November from the letter, which was shared with it. The letter says it appears that the Chief Electoral Officer's office filed these appeals in April 2026 although each of these electors had been checked and included in the rolls by judicial officers. It cites the Commission's counter affidavit in the Supreme Court in October (court-52), which, as The Wire gives it, says in paragraph 63 that officers of the Chief Electoral Officer's office filed the appeals and in paragraph 60 that these electors' documents are on the portal with a favourable order of the judicial officer. Sircar asks how more than 12 lakh appeals carrying a single batch code for 5 April could have been filed in one day, what part the Commission's IT division played, and whether the processing of names for deletion was decided by the Commission's IT system. He asks how appeals against 599 electors in Hemtabad, Uttar Dinajpur, could carry the batch code of 5 April when the supplementary list that cleared them was published on 6 April, a finding The Wire first reported (court-58). He also asks whether the special drive for left-out electors is open to everyone missing from the roll before the revision or only to those on the list of absent, shifted, dead and duplicate electors. He writes that the Commission's letter of 1 October, which told booth level officers to compare the current roll with the roll before the revision, would cover 27.16 lakh electors deleted by judicial officers and 5.46 lakh deleted through Form 7. The Commission's letter and the Chief Electoral Officer's press note of 7 October both say that anyone whose name has been deleted can apply for enrolment at any time, and he asks whether that includes the roughly 22 lakh electors who have appealed to the tribunals, and whether an Electoral Registration Officer can enrol an elector deleted by judicial officers whose appeal is pending. He writes that the Chief Electoral Officer had neither acknowledged nor answered his first letter, of 22 October, in three weeks.
items.quote: So, who ordered these appeals to disenfranchise so many lakhs and why
items.response: The Wire says it has written to the West Bengal Chief Electoral Officer's office several times in recent weeks about the appeals, the electors still under adjudication and the special drive, and will update the report on a reply. It reports that the Commission has told the Supreme Court that the appeals were filed by officers of the Chief Electoral Officer's office 'in their capacity as authorities under the RP Act', with authority under the Court's orders, and that 'these matters were not brought to the commission', and that the Commission has not named the officers or given the grounds of the appeals.

items.headline: INDIA bloc seeks SC nod to question EC members over SIR, submits 48 queries
items.claim: INDIA bloc leaders asked the Supreme Court on 16 November 2026 for permission to put 48 written questions, known as interrogatories, to the Election Commission, Business Standard reported. The Congress announced the application in a post on X and published with it 17 pages of the filing, headed Annexure A-1, Interrogatories on behalf of the Petitioners. The filing names who is to answer each question on affidavit. They are Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu, whom it describes as the deponent of the Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October (court-52) and of its supplementary affidavit of 14 November (court-76), the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and the Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, who are to answer from their own knowledge, including their own approval, participation, objection, dissent or concurrence, and the Commission's Director General (IT). Where a question is put to more than one person, each is to answer it on a separate affidavit. The questions are grouped in ten parts. They ask on what date and by what means each of the three Commissioners approved the filing of the counter affidavit, and in which file and on what date the Commission took the decision, recited in its order of 24 June 2025, to begin the revision in the entire country. They ask whether the order of the Commission's first appellate authority in an RTI appeal, which said the Commission had so far taken no decision on a revision across the country in 2025, was correct when it was made. They ask on how many occasions between 19 February 2025 and 26 October 2026 Sandhu or Joshi recorded in writing an objection, dissent or reservation on the revision, ECINET, Form 6 or the filing of appeals, and whether any decision on the revision was taken by majority under Section 18(2) of the 2023 Act. Other parts concern the office order of 28 July 2026 and the two Election Commissioners' joint direction of 30 July, the appeals filed in West Bengal against electors included by judicial officers, the accounts that can add, delete, modify or restore entries in the electoral roll database and whether ECINET's audit trail since 24 June 2025 is intact, the 97 Goa electors, the declaration added to the online Form 6, objections in Form 7, the office order of 4 November and the letters of 3 and 6 November annexed to the supplementary affidavit, and whether approvals given by electronic means were sought or conveyed by e-mail, WhatsApp or another messaging application. The Congress said in its post that the Commission's affidavit had not answered a single question raised on what the party calls Vote Chori. Bar and Bench reported that Rahul Gandhi and ten other opposition leaders moved the application. It names the eleven as the petitioners who filed the petition in October. They are Rahul Gandhi, Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge, Saugata Roy of the Trinamool Congress, Samajwadi Party President Akhilesh Yadav, Tejashwi Prasad Yadav of the Rashtriya Janata Dal, Sanjay Raut of the Shiv Sena (UBT), M.A. Baby of the CPI(M), D. Raja of the CPI, Mahua Majhi of the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha, Supriya Sule of the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar) and Mohammed Basheer of the IUML. PTI, in The Tribune, reported that the application was filed in Rahul Gandhi's pending petition. Bar and Bench reported that the application seeks permission under Order V Rule 1, Order XXXVIII Rule 11(9) and Order LV Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 to serve the interrogatories. It reported that the petitioners rely on the Constitution Bench judgment in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India for the point that the Court may require officials to answer specific questions where facts central to a constitutional challenge lie within the exclusive knowledge of an authority administering a technological system. It reported that the application asks that, if the Commission claims privilege over any official record, it be directed to state the specific grounds for each record so that the Court can decide the claim. It also reported that the interrogatories seek state-wise data on electors dropped from the draft and final rolls. The Supreme Court's cause list for 17 November 2026 lists the batch, led by W.P.(C) No. 1246 of 2026, as item 26 before the bench of the Chief Justice, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana, with W.P.(C) No. 1351 of 2026, Rahul Gandhi and others against the Election Commission of India and others, as item 26.5.
items.quote: Where an interrogatory is directed to more than one person, each such person shall answer it on a separate affidavit.
items.response: The interrogatories can be served only if the Court allows the application, and no order on it had been reported. The Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October said that the three SIR orders were unanimous decisions of the Commission and that a suggestion, observation or query by a member while a file moves is not a decision of the Commission (court-52). No reply by the Commission to the application was reported.

items.case: Rahul Gandhi v. Election Commission of India, W.P.(C) No. 1351 of 2026, item 26.5 in the batch led by W.P.(C) No. 1246 of 2026, Supreme Court (court-42, court-43, court-52, court-78)
items.headline: No Material Evidence to Show SIR Was EC’s ‘Unanimous’ Decision, Rahul Gandhi Tells Supreme Court
items.claim: Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders have told the Supreme Court in a rejoinder to the Election Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October (court-52) that the Commission gave no proof of its claim that the SIR was a unanimous decision of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, The Wire reported on 16 November 2026. The rejoinder says the counter affidavit gives no particulars or dates of that approval, and that the Court should not take into account "a bare assertion of unanimous decision of the Election Commissioners without perusal of the relevant recorded files". It says the affidavit does not explain when the decision to hold the revision across the country was taken, where it was recorded, or how the Commission's RTI replies that no such decision had been taken are to be reconciled with its order of 24 June 2025. It says the affidavit was signed by a Deputy Election Commissioner on behalf of the three members, who are all senior to him, and that a general statement by an administrative officer cannot take the place of the primary records or of the members' own explanation. It says that Sandhu and Joshi writing to the Cabinet Secretary is "itself inconsistent with the picture of unanimous functioning" that the Commission presents. On Form 6 it says that calling the declaration a separate component does not change the fact that an applicant using the online Form 6 process "was required to encounter and complete the additional declaration as part of that process". The Wire reports that the petitioners say 97 electors in Goa were deleted and could not be added back because local electoral officials could not get into the software to enrol them again, and that the Commission's affidavit said 88 were added back through Form 6 applications. Bar and Bench reported the same affidavit as saying 88 of the 97 had since applied through Form 6 (court-52). The rejoinder says the affidavit "does not deny that the software lacked a facility to restore these electors". It says the office order of 1997 on which the Commission relies does not cover the design of the roll software, changes to statutory forms or application procedures, or the bringing of litigation or appeals. On the appeals filed by officers of the West Bengal Chief Electoral Officer against electors the tribunals had cleared, it says that if they were acts of the Commission, "the respondents must disclose the decision of the commission authorising the same, together with the relevant approval and delegation records". The Hindu reported the same day that Rahul Gandhi had told the Court that the Commission produced no proof that the SIR was a unanimous decision of the three members, and that the Commission's affidavit of 26 October answered a petition by INDIA bloc leaders led by him. The Wire gives the hearing as 17 November before a bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, and the Supreme Court's cause list for that day lists the petition as item 26.5 (court-78).
items.quote: "No minutes of the meeting, file notings, recorded approvals, agenda, deliberations or other primary material evidencing the participation and approval of all three members have been produced with the counter-affidavit," the rejoinder says.
items.response: These are the petitioners' submissions in a rejoinder, as The Wire reports them. The Commission's counter affidavit of 26 October said that the three SIR orders were unanimous decisions of the Commission, that Form 6 has not been amended and the SIR declaration is a separate document, and that the West Bengal appeals were filed by officers of the state Chief Electoral Officer under the Court's orders and were not placed before the Commission (court-52). No reply by the Commission to the rejoinder was reported, and the Court had made no finding on any of these points.

items.headline: Rahul Gandhi's plea to serve 48 interrogatories on ECI: Supreme Court to decide after considering ECI's objections
items.claim: A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said on 17 November 2026 that the matter will be heard on 9 December after the Election Commission files its objections to the application by Rahul Gandhi and ten other opposition leaders for leave to serve 48 interrogatories on the Commission (court-78), Bar and Bench reported. The Chief Justice told the Commission's counsel that it may file its reply and raise its objections, and said the Court would examine the interrogatories and then decide. Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal appeared for Rahul Gandhi. The Indian Express reported in its live coverage that the Court adjourned the hearing of the batch of petitions on the Commission's functioning and that the petitions will now be taken up on 9 December. Amar Ujala reported that the hearing on the petitions of Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders was put off to 9 December. No order on the application was reported.
items.quote: "We will examine the interrogatories issue and then take a call," the CJI added.

items.case: Electors in West Bengal whose cases are still under adjudication after the judicial review the Supreme Court ordered, and the Chief Electoral Officer's letters on the judicial officers' logins (court-59, court-75)
items.headline: ‘Can’t appeal, can’t vote’: The forgotten voters of Bengal SIR
items.claim: Electors in West Bengal whose eligibility went before judicial officers and is still marked under adjudication have not reached the appellate tribunals, The Indian Express reported on 17 November 2026. The paper puts their number, from unnamed sources, at over 25,000 in Murshidabad, Malda, Nadia and Howrah, and says poll officials admitted they were not sure of the total. The state's Additional Chief Electoral Officer wrote to district election officers on 29 October about reactivating the login IDs of judicial officers to dispose of cases in which the decision and the e-signing were pending, and asked for the status of disposal by 3 November. The paper reports that at polling station 44, in ward 21 of the Samserganj constituency in Murshidabad, 590 of the 949 electors left on the roll after the names marked dead and displaced were removed, 62%, are still under adjudication. The booth level officer of part 192 in Farakka told the paper that 799 of the 1,372 electors in his part are still under adjudication, and that the assistant electoral registration officer and other officials told the booth level officers they were helpless and to go to court. An elector in Dhulian told the paper that he would have appealed to the tribunals had his name been deleted, that he can neither appeal nor vote, and that his family's last hearing was on 30 January, at the Dhulian Municipality office. The paper says the others under adjudication have been waiting for word since December 2025 or January. Another elector in Dhulian, a primary schoolteacher who was on poll duty in the Assembly election, said she could not vote in it.
items.quote: “These are cases which were not properly disposed of by judicial officers. We have informed the Calcutta HC about this because in such cases we can’t take any step as per court orders. Only judicial officers can take action.”
items.response: A senior official in the Chief Electoral Officer's office, whom the paper does not name, said the office had informed the Calcutta High Court and that the Chief Electoral Officer had informed the Election Commission. The Additional Chief Electoral Officer, Arindam Niyogi, said only the court could decide the cases. The paper could not reach the Chief Electoral Officer, Neelam Meena. Krishanu Mitra of the Trinamool Congress blamed the Union Government, Sujan Chakraborty of the CPI(M) said the government now decides through the Commission who will vote, Soumya Aich Roy of the Congress said the Commission had carried out targeted exclusion, and Ritesh Tiwary, a BJP MLA, said it was for the Commission to answer.

items.case: Network of Women in Media, India v. Union of India and others, W.P.(C) No. 1361 of 2026, and connected petitions on the police's treatment of journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October, Supreme Court (court-36, court-62)
items.headline: Reel Makers Not Entitled To Journalistic Protection During Protests, Delhi Police To Supreme Court
items.claim: The Delhi Police told the Supreme Court in a counter-affidavit that the Court's direction of 11 October protecting journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, does not extend to reel-makers and social media influencers, LiveLaw and Bar and Bench reported. The affidavit answers petitions by the Network of Women in Media, India, the Free Speech Collective, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Kerala Union of Working Journalists on the police's treatment of journalists at the protests. LiveLaw reports that the order of 11 October recorded the Solicitor General's assurance that lawyers, journalists and other professionals would not be hindered in their professional duties. The police said the direction protects journalists in the discharge of their duties and was not meant to exempt reel-makers, influencers or unruly elements from the general law or from lawful police directions at the site of a prohibited assembly, and that whether reel-makers can be treated as journalists is yet to be determined. Bar and Bench reports that the affidavit accepts that independent media persons, freelancers and people reporting on YouTube or other digital platforms may gather and publish news without accreditation or a press card, and says they remain subject to the general law and to lawful police directions. On the complaints of sexual harassment by a police officer at the protest near Jantar Mantar on 3 October, Bar and Bench reports the affidavit as saying that two of the three journalists who complained did not wish to pursue their complaints, that the third did not join the inquiry, that CCTV footage showed no act of sexual harassment, and that the three complaints have been filed and the matter closed. LiveLaw reports the affidavit as saying that four complaints were received from women journalists after the protests of 3 October and sent to the Crime Branch, and that the CCTV footage did not corroborate the specific allegations. The police answered other journalists' allegations of obstruction and detention one by one, denied seizing any journalist's equipment and asked the Court to dismiss the petitions, Bar and Bench reported. LiveLaw reports the affidavit as saying that any journalist removed from a protest site by mistake was released as soon as their credentials were verified.
items.quote: The said direction protects journalists in the discharge of their professional duties and does not, and was not intended to, exempt the so-called reel-makers and social media influencers or unruly elements from the operation of the general law or from compliance with the lawful directions of the Law Enforcement Agencies at the site of a prohibited assembly.
items.response: The affidavit is the police's reply to the petitions. LiveLaw reports that the police defended their advisory of 5 October asking journalists covering protests to carry an identity card from their organisation or an accreditation card, and said that the absence of accreditation would not by itself stop a journalist being identified. No reply from the petitioners and no hearing date were reported.

items.case: An advocate's application under section 175(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita for an FIR against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and others, magistrate's court, Delhi
items.headline: Delhi Police seeks more time to probe voter suppression allegations against CEC Gyanesh Kumar
items.claim: The Delhi Police submitted an action taken report to a magistrate's court on 17 November 2026 on an advocate's application for an FIR against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, and others, and asked for more time to complete its inquiry, The New Indian Express and Dainik Jagran reported. The advocate had applied under section 175(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, under which a magistrate can order an investigation, and the magistrate had asked the police for the report. items.headline: Delhi SIR : Supreme Court Asks ECI To Verify Complaint Of False Form 7s Filed To Delete Mustafabad Voters
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana disposed of the petition by Ali Mehdi, the Congress candidate for Mustafabad in 2025, on Form 7 objections in Mustafabad (court-81) on 19 November 2026, LiveLaw and Bar and Bench reported. The bench directed the Election Commission and Delhi's Chief Electoral Officer to verify the petitioner's allegations and take the necessary remedial measures strictly in accordance with law, and expressed no opinion on the merits. The petition, citing newspaper reports, said that 28 electors against whom deletion applications had been filed were found living at their addresses, and counsel for the petitioner told the Court that the authorities had accepted that 36 of the 37 objections filed in the name of one booth level agent were false (form7-62). He said the police had not registered an FIR on the petitioner's complaint, and asked that no name be deleted on a Form 7 without the prescribed notices to the objector and to the elector. The bench said that the Commission's power over a booth level agent, who is an agent of a political party, goes no further than blacklisting one who makes a fraudulent application. LiveLaw gives that remark to Justice Bagchi and Bar and Bench to the Chief Justice. LiveLaw reports that Justice Bagchi told the petitioner to approach the magistrate for an FIR. Bar and Bench reports the Chief Justice as saying that the complaint should name the booth level agents concerned so that remedial and, if necessary, disciplinary steps can be taken, and the bench as saying that the petitioner can make a representation to the Commission.
items.quote: Since the petitioner has already submitted a representation, we dispose of the writ petition, without expressing any opinion, with a direction to the authorities to verify the allegation and take necessary remedial measures strictly in accordance with law
items.response: The reports give no submission by the Commission or the Chief Electoral Officer at the hearing. items.case: Anjali Bhardwaj and another v. Election Commission of India and others, W.P.(C) No. 1188 of 2026, an interlocutory application by the petitioners on Delhi's revision, Supreme Court (court-54, court-60, court-61, form7-61)
items.headline: Delhi SIR : Petitioners Cite Report On Form 7 Misuse, Seek Supreme Court Directions
items.claim: Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, the petitioners in the Supreme Court case on Delhi's revision (court-54, court-61), have filed an interlocutory application asking the Court to extend the timeline of Delhi's revision and to direct the Election Commission to carry out its instructions of 6 November on electors in the ASDD list, those marked absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, LiveLaw, The Tribune and The New Indian Express reported on 18 November 2026. The application says 47,56,722 electors in Delhi were placed in that list. It says Delhi's Chief Electoral Officer continues to direct these electors to Form 6, that he has issued no standard operating procedure or instructions to registration officers and booth level officers for the new mechanism, and that the Commission has announced no revised timeline. It asks the Court to direct the Commission to implement the instructions of 6 November and file a compliance report, to let every elector in Delhi's ASDD list submit an enumeration form and have the earlier EPIC number restored whether or not the elector has already filed Form 6, and to publish constituency-wise and consolidated figures of these electors who have submitted enumeration forms and of those restored to the roll. On Form 7, the application cites The Hindu's report that 787 objections seeking the deletion of Muslim electors in Mustafabad were filed in the names of 20 booth level agents of the BJP, at least 16 of whom denied filing or authorising them (form7-60). It asks for an impartial inquiry into the use of Form 7 in Mustafabad and other areas, for FIRs wherever cognisable offences such as forgery, criminal impersonation and identity fraud are disclosed, and for action under section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 against anyone found to have knowingly made a false declaration. It also asks for an audit of every Form 7 filed in Delhi during the revision to check whether the objectors named authorised and signed them, for every Form 7 to be disclosed publicly, for periodic audits, physical verification of objections and checks on the identity of objectors, and for a booth level agent who files a Form 7 to declare that status, to be shown in the Form 10 disclosures.
items.quote: The petitioners have sought directions to the ECI to ensure that all Form 7 objections are publicly disclosed and that every Booth Level Agent filing an objection expressly identifies their status as a BLA. They have further sought a direction that this status be reflected in the corresponding Form 10 disclosures.
items.response: The reports give no reply from the Commission or the Chief Electoral Officer and no date on which the application will be heard. The petition was listed for admission on 19 November with two applications (list-06). At that listing the bench posted it to 2 December and asked the Commission for the number of enumeration forms and of Form 6, Form 7 and Form 8 applications (court-89). The reports of that hearing do not give this application's number or say whether the bench passed an order on it.

items.case: Pleas by the Government of Karnataka and Karnataka's State Election Commission on the elections to the five city corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority, Supreme Court (court-73)
items.headline: Allow Bengaluru civic polls on old rolls: Karnataka, State Election Commission to Supreme Court
items.claim: The Government of Karnataka and the State Election Commission have asked the Supreme Court to allow the elections to the five city corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority to be held on the ward-wise rolls published on 18 April 2026, before the Election Commission's revision of the rolls in the state, The Indian Express reported on 19 November 2026 (court-73). The state government's plea says that by the final roll the Election Commission published on 27 October the electorate of Bengaluru fell from about 1.03 crore to 59.08 lakh, and calls this a mass deletion of over 43 lakh names in the Greater Bengaluru area. The State Election Commission told the Court that the rolls of 18 April list 88,95,361 electors in the five corporations, and that the Election Commission's final rolls for the 28 Assembly constituencies in Bengaluru district list 59,08,151 electors with the rural areas and 51,87,575 without them. It said the Election Commission had not shared the authenticated database of the final roll more than three weeks after its publication, and that it would need two months from receiving the data to prepare ward-wise rolls. It said that if it may use the rolls of 18 April it will complete the elections on or before 31 January 2027, and the state has asked for the Court's deadline of 31 December 2026 to be extended to that date. The State Election Commission had written to the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, on 19 September that if work began only after the final publication on 27 October it would be extremely difficult to prepare the rolls and hold the elections within December 2026.
items.quote: As per the final electoral roll published by the ECI on 27.10.2026, the electorate in the city of Bengaluru has plummeted from approximately 1.03 crore voters to just 59.08 lakh voters, resulting in a staggering mass deletion of over 43 lakh names within the Greater Bengaluru Area alone
items.response: The report gives no reply from the Election Commission and no date of hearing. The Times of India reported on 18 November that the Greater Bengaluru Authority had announced the schedule of the special summary revision, with the draft roll on 1 December, claims and objections until 31 December and the final roll on 20 January 2027, and that the State Election Commission has said the revision will not affect the schedule of the corporation elections.

items.case: Kirana Committee Delhi and another v. Union of India and others, W.P.(C) No. 1395 of 2026, the traders' petition on the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner and on Ramlila Maidan as a protest site, Supreme Court (protest-47, court-35, court-36)
items.headline: Supreme Court Issues Notice To CJP, Congress, AAP & AISA On Delhi Traders' Plea Against Protests
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana issued notice on 18 November 2026 to the Cockroach Janta Party, the Congress, the Aam Aadmi Party and the All India Students' Association on a petition by two traders' associations, the Kirana Committee Delhi and the Delhi Iron and Hardware Merchant Association, which say that the protests these organisations held in Delhi in October against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, hurt their business, LiveLaw reported. Hindustan Times reports that the bench also sought replies from the Centre and the Delhi government. On 3 November the Court had asked whether the organisers of the protests had been made parties, and the associations then added them. The petition was first raised in the Court on 16 October (protest-47). Their counsel, Mukul Rohatgi, objected to the designation of Ramlila Maidan as a protest venue. Hindustan Times reports that the petition asks for the Delhi Police's order of 11 October designating Ramlila Maidan as a protest site to be quashed and for a fresh, reasoned assessment. It puts Delhi's daily business at about Rs 500 crore to Rs 600 crore, of which it says about Rs 250 crore was at risk each day in the peak season from October 2026 to January 2027. The associations say they are not asking for a ban on peaceful protests. They ask for a framework for the location, duration and scale of demonstrations and for continued access to markets, homes, hospitals and public transport. The bench said the petition can be heard with MA Baby v. Union of India and the connected petitions on the restrictions imposed during the protests (court-35), which are tentatively listed on 27 November, and that it will take the contempt petitions against the police and other authorities separately on another day (court-36).
items.quote: The bench stated that the traders' petition can be posted along with the other petitions (MA Baby v Union of India and connected matters) which question the restrictions imposed by the authorities in the wake of protests. Those matters are tentatively listed on November 27.
items.response: The Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, told the Court that the petition should be heard with the petitions on the police action during the protests, because the traders' rights and the right to protest are contesting rights, Hindustan Times reported. No reply from the parties and organisations named had been reported.

items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana heard Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri's petition on Delhi's revision on 19 November 2026 and posted it to 2 December, Hindustan Times, The Times of India and The Indian Express reported. The bench asked the Election Commission's counsel, Dama Seshadri Naidu, to say how many enumeration forms had been filled and how many Form 6, Form 7 and Form 8 applications had been made, and said that on the cut-off date it would consider whether the facility to use these forms had been provided, Hindustan Times reported. The Times of India reports that the figures asked for are of the enumeration forms and the Forms 6 and 8 received and approved between 30 October and 30 November, and The Hindu, in the standfirst of its report, that the Court asked for the number of applications received for the inclusion, deletion and correction of names. The reports name different deadlines. Hindustan Times says the petition seeks to extend 25 November, the last date for claims and objections in Delhi. The Times of India says the Court may extend 30 November, and the headline of The Hindu's report gives 30 November as the deadline for electors to be included again. Under the Commission's letter of 17 November, as Hindustan Times reported it, 30 November is also the last day for handing out and collecting the enumeration forms of electors left off the draft roll as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate. items.case: West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals of retired judges (court-18, court-67)
items.headline: Fresh hurdle for SIR tribunal: Staff go on strike after salary non-payment
items.claim: Twelve housekeeping staff of West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals at Joka in Kolkata went on strike on 19 November because their salaries had not been paid, The Times of India reported. It was the second time in November that they stopped work. They have worked for four months and been paid for one, and a source told the paper that the current staff have worked since July and were paid only for September, before Durga Puja. Their monthly salary is Rs 14,500, a source said. The agency that employs them told them that the state had not paid it. The paper reports from sources in the tribunals that the drivers of the cars that carry the judges have also not been paid, because the agencies that supply the cars have received nothing, and that several drivers have left. Each judge's car, a Toyota Innova, was hired for Rs 1,20,000 a month, and the payments have not been made. The four buses that bring secretarial and office staff from Howrah, Sealdah, Baruipur and Diamond Harbour have not been paid for either. A source said that the state government's Home and Hill Affairs Department is to make the payments and the Commission to reimburse them, and that it is not known why the payments stopped. The 19 tribunals were set up by the Commission in March on the Supreme Court's orders, and the judges sit at the campus of the Syama Prasad Mookerjee National Institute of Water and Sanitation at Joka.

items.case: Network of Women in Media, India v. Union of India and others, W.P.(C) No. 1361 of 2026, and connected petitions on the police's treatment of journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October, Supreme Court (court-36, court-62, court-83)
items.headline: Anti-SIR protest: Journalists dispute Delhi Police’s affidavit to Supreme Court
items.claim: Newslaundry set the accounts of journalists detained during the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October against the Delhi Police's counter-affidavit in the Supreme Court (court-83), in a report of 20 November. The affidavit says some journalists were mistakenly identified as protesters in the absence of conspicuously displayed identification or accreditation, and that each was released as soon as their credentials were ascertained. Newslaundry reports journalists saying they were released only after a senior officer phoned or when a vehicle broke down. The affidavit says Ryan Thomas of The Caravan was not detained or kept at any holding facility on 11 October and was merely removed from the site, and that the medico-legal case is under investigation. Thomas told Newslaundry that he was holding up his press card when he was put in a detention bus, and that he was beaten in the bus and then in a jeep. He obtained a medico-legal certificate at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, which Newslaundry says does not record that the police caused the injury. He said he had filed no FIR and would send the police a legal notice. Ayush Tiwari of Scroll said he was detained at 11 am on 10 October while wearing his press card and could leave after about an hour and a half, when the bus he was in caught fire near Paharganj police station. Newslaundry says three of its reporters and an intern were detained on 10 October. One of them, Ashwine Singh, said he showed the police his card and that this happened between 11:30 am and noon. Newslaundry says its reporters were released after a senior officer called about their identity, and puts the whole incident at about three to four hours. Suhail Muhammad of 24 News said he and his cameraperson were driven around for about 30 minutes before the bus stopped in Connaught Place and they could leave. The affidavit calls false the petitioners' contention that the police arbitrarily seized media equipment. Rajwinder Singh and Lakhwinder Singh, who run the channel The Mike Report, said the police took their camera, that it took them at least three to four days to get it back, and that they were given no seizure memo. On the complaints of four women journalists, Newslaundry reports the police as saying the inquiry was concluded for lack of corroboration, and says one complainant has gone to court.
items.quote: Some journalists were mistakenly identified as protestors in the absence of conspicuously displayed identification/accreditation. However, the moment the journalistic credentials of any person were ascertained, such a person was immediately released.
items.response: The affidavit is the police's reply to the petitions, and the journalists' accounts are their own. Newslaundry says it asked the Delhi Police's public relations officer and the Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi, for a response and would update its report when one came.

The lawyer for one of them gave a date in December for a hearing before a magistrate, which is not carried, because it concerns a private complainant's case. items.headline: Deleted Kolkata voters pin hopes as SIR judge resumes regular hearing
items.claim: The retired Calcutta High Court judge Kanchan Chakraborty, appointed about two months ago to West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunal that hears appeals from Kolkata, resumed office in the past week and began hearing appeals, The Times of India reported on 22 November. The paper says the hearing and disposal of Kolkata's appeals had been erratic since the first judge appointed to it, the former Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court T.S. Sivagnanam, resigned in May. items.case: Network of Women in Media, India v. Union of India and others, W.P.(C) No. 1361 of 2026, and connected petitions on the police's treatment of journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October, Supreme Court (court-36, court-62, court-83, court-91)
items.headline: ‘Catalogue of admissions’: Journalists’ body says Delhi Police affidavit admits the interference it denies
items.claim: The Network of Women in Media, India filed a rejoinder in the Supreme Court on 21 November to the Delhi Police's counter-affidavit (court-83) in its petition on the police's treatment of journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in October, Newslaundry, LiveLaw, The New Indian Express and Scroll reported. It says the affidavit itself reveals the extent of the interference complained of, and Newslaundry reports it as saying that paragraphs of the affidavit read like a catalogue of admissions and that terms such as mistaken identity, verification and released upon identification soften the description of actual restraint. LiveLaw reports it as arguing that the police's own account, that journalists were removed from protest sites, put in police vehicles for verification and released once identified, establishes the interference with their liberty and their work, and that their eventual release does not answer whether the restraint was lawful. On the police's reliance on section 172 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the rejoinder says the power arises only where a person disobeys an earlier lawful direction, and that the affidavit does not identify, incident by incident, the direction given, the officer who gave it, what the journalist did to disobey it or why removal was needed in place of a less restrictive measure. LiveLaw reports it as citing section 65 of the Delhi Police Act and the Supreme Court's judgment in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal on the safeguards of arrest and detention, and Newslaundry reports it as saying that section 29 of that Act only names the officers who can issue orders regulating assemblies and public places. The rejoinder calls the police's use of the term reel-makers a retrospective justification, says the question is what the person was doing, and says the freedom to gather news cannot be made conditional on accreditation, employment with a recognised media organisation or an employer's identity card. On the complaints of sexual harassment from the protest of 3 October, which the police say the Crime Branch closed, it says the closure reinforces the case for an inquiry independent of the police whose personnel are complained against, and that a complainant's reluctance to pursue a complaint is no conclusive proof that the conduct did not occur. LiveLaw reports that it also cites the National Human Rights Commission's notice of 8 October to the Delhi Police Commissioner on the reported harassment of three women journalists. The police had said that 3,747 women personnel were deployed by day and 664 at night and that women taken away in police vehicles were accompanied by a woman officer, and the rejoinder says these figures do not identify who handled the women journalists. It says the police could have set up press areas, liaison officers, safe routes and protective helmets at a protest planned in advance, asks the Court to reject the police's plea to dismiss the petitions, and seeks safeguards, independent scrutiny and the production of contemporaneous records.
items.quote: The police cannot justify an interference with personal liberty simply by refraining from calling it a detention or arrest.
items.response: The rejoinder is the petitioner's answer to the police's affidavit. None of the reports carries a reply from the Delhi Police or gives a date for the next hearing.

items.case: W.P.(C) No. 1089 of 2025 and connected petitions (SIR matters related to the State of West Bengal), on West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals, Supreme Court (court-18, court-38, court-47, court-67, court-92)
items.headline: West Bengal SIR | Defer Appeals Against Inclusions, Prioritise Appeals Filed By Deleted Voters : Supreme Court To Appellate Tribunals
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana directed West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals on 23 November 2026 to divide the appeals before them into two groups, the appeals of electors whose names were deleted and the appeals against the inclusion of names, and to give the first group preference in final disposal, LiveLaw, Hindustan Times and The Times of India reported. The order says the appeals against inclusion involve no urgency and may for the time being be deferred. The Court directed that among the appeals of deleted electors those from the constituencies of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation be given priority, because the municipal elections are due. LiveLaw and Hindustan Times report that it directed the Election Commission to increase the strength of the tribunals in consultation with the Calcutta High Court, which Hindustan Times gives as the High Court's Chief Justice. The Times of India reports the direction as one to the High Court's Chief Justice, in consultation with the Commission, to increase the number of tribunals from the present 19. The Court asked the Commission to find other premises for the tribunals at different places in Kolkata. Hindustan Times reports that of the 38.31 lakh appeals filed, 22.21 lakh are by electors seeking to have their names restored and 16.10 lakh challenge inclusions, and that the 16.10 lakh were filed by officials of the office of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer. Prashant Bhushan, for the petitioners, told the bench that only a little over one lakh appeals had been decided and that 93% of those decided had gone in favour of the deleted electors, Hindustan Times and LiveLaw reported. The Times of India reports him as saying that more than 90% of the 1.4 lakh appeals decided had been allowed. He said that more than two lakh electors from the Kolkata municipal area had been excluded and that their appeals were pending. The senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan argued that the Chief Electoral Officer had no authority in law to file the appeals against inclusion, because under Rule 23 an appeal from a registration officer's decision lies to an officer the Commission designates, and LiveLaw reports him calling it an appeal from the Election Commission to itself.
items.quote: The second set of appeals does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred. The first set of appeals shall be given preference in the matter of final disposal,
items.response: Hindustan Times reports that the Commission's affidavit of October in the Supreme Court said the appeals against inclusion were filed by officers of the Chief Electoral Officer's office in their statutory capacity under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and that the matters had not been brought before the Commission, and that the affidavit did not identify anyone who authorised them. items.case: Application by Prasenjit Bose in W.P.(C) No. 1089 of 2025 and connected petitions (SIR matters related to the State of West Bengal), on welfare benefits for deleted electors, Supreme Court (court-95)
items.headline: Petitioner Urges Supreme Court To Clarify SIR Deletion Won't Lead To Denial Of State Welfare Benefits
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana issued notice on 23 November 2026 on an application by Prasenjit Bose, who chairs the SIR panel of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee, in the West Bengal SIR matter, LiveLaw reported. The application asks the Court to direct the state to withdraw all notifications restricting the access of electors deleted in the revision to welfare benefits, and names the Annapurna Yojana, the Public Distribution System and OBC certificates. The Times of India reports that the Court asked the state government to respond to the allegation that electors deleted in the revision are being denied rations and benefits under welfare schemes. Gopal Sankaranarayanan and Prashant Bhushan, for the petitioners, said the state government was taking the entitlements away. Justice Bagchi said the Court had already clarified that exclusion from the roll should not affect other entitlements, called the complaint an independent cause of action and suggested that it be raised in a separate writ petition. Sankaranarayanan pointed to a state notification of 4 June providing that beneficiaries of the Public Distribution System be verified and deleted on the basis of the revision's outcome, and Bhushan said that the Chief Minister of West Bengal had said deleted electors would be deprived of the benefits. Justice Bagchi said that this was in the nature of a statement by a political person and that an individual who was actually deprived could approach the High Court, and the Chief Justice said that any person affected could approach the High Court. The petitioners asked for a one-line clarification from the Court in place of fresh litigation in the High Court.
items.quote: But if there's an actual deprivation of any individual he is at liberty to approach the High Court. We have clarified that
items.response: The Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, said that bald assertions unaccompanied by facts should not be made for political purposes, LiveLaw reported, and The Times of India reports him saying that the petitioners had not cited a single example. Justice Bagchi replied that there was no bald assertion because the petitioners were pointing to a government notification, and said the Court would see whether it was being given effect. D.S. Naidu, for the Commission, said the Court had already made such observations many times. No report gives a date for the state's reply.

items.case: The State of West Bengal and another v. Dipu Das and others, the state government's appeal against the Calcutta High Court division bench's order on the Kolkata Municipal Corporation elections and the delimitation of its wards, Supreme Court (court-37, court-38, court-95)
items.headline: SC ‘inclined’ to stay Calcutta HC order deferring civic polls till decision on ward delimitation
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said on 25 November 2026 that it was inclined to stay an order of a Calcutta High Court division bench that restrained West Bengal's State Election Commission from issuing a notification for the Kolkata Municipal Corporation elections until a single judge decides a challenge to the delimitation of the corporation's wards, PTI reported. The delimitation may raise the number of wards from 144 to 209. The bench said the writ petition before the single judge would be directed to be transferred to the division bench, which would pass a fresh order, and it asked the Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, to seek instructions by 30 November. LawTrend reports that the bench also indicated that the elections could remain on hold until the division bench forms a view, and that the Court has not yet stayed the High Court's order. The petitioner in the High Court, Dipu Das, a former councillor of the CPI(M), alleged that the delimitation exercise was undertaken on the basis of electoral rolls instead of the actual population, and so left a substantial number of residents out of consideration. He asked the High Court to declare the whole exercise of fixing the number of wards void and to quash the gazette notification of 11 September expanding the wards. He also said the corporation had no elected council and that its former chairperson had been appointed its administrator after the House was dissolved on 8 June. The single judge refused an interim stay on 29 October and Das appealed to the division bench. PTI reports the division bench's order as saying that the state government could allow its chosen administrator to make a tailor-made recommendation and then be bound by it, in effect allowing the government to recommend amendments to itself, and that section 601 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act vests in the corporation the power to make a binding recommendation on the delimitation of its own wards. The order said its observations were tentative as far as the final disposal of the writ petition was concerned.
items.quote: We shouldn’t postpone pending elections unreasonably.
items.response: Neither PTI nor LawTrend gives a submission on the merits by the state government, the State Election Commission or the petitioner at this hearing. The Election Commission is not reported as a party. PTI gives 30 November as the date by which the Solicitor General is to seek instructions, and LawTrend says the Court will consider the matter further after that. Neither gives a time or an item number for a hearing.

items.case: The petitions alleging illegal detention of protesters during the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October, Supreme Court (court-36, court-83, protest-40)
items.headline: Supreme Court seeks Centre's response to petitions over detentions during October protest against CEC

items.case: West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals of retired judges (court-18, court-67, court-90, court-92, court-95)
items.headline: Work-from-home option for Bengal SIR tribunals: Efficiency cited on hearings
items.claim: The judges of West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals have been given the option of working from home, The Telegraph reported on 25 November 2026, citing sources it does not name. Business Today reported the same day, following The Telegraph. A source in the tribunal told the paper that the judges had received calls from what the source called the state election commission, through the nodal officers for the tribunals, asking whether they would be comfortable working from home. The tribunals sit at SPM-Niwas, a central government institute at Joka on the southern edge of Kolkata, and the paper says several judges have complained of the long commute. It says at least a couple of judges are reported to have said they would work from home if the poll panel arranged suitable infrastructure and enough staff. An official said one judge who spends four hours travelling between his home and Joka welcomed the option but said it had to be backed by adequate staff and their transport to and from his home. A source attached to one of the 19 tribunals said its presiding judge could not hear more than 10 to 12 appeals a day because of logistical problems, and an official said the judge starts work around 11 am and that work ends by 4.30 pm because the staff have to leave. The paper says four buses carry the tribunals' staff between Joka and Howrah, Sealdah, Baruipur and Diamond Harbour (court-90). Officials in the tribunals said the judges would for now hear only the appeals against the removal of names. The Supreme Court directed on 23 November that those appeals be given preference (court-95).

items.response: The account of the option and of the tribunals' working day comes from sources and officials the papers do not name, and the report gives no statement from the Chief Electoral Officer, the State Election Commission or the Election Commission. items.case: Kerala Union of Working Journalists v. Union of India, W.P.(C) No. 1373 of 2026, on the police's treatment of journalists covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in October, Supreme Court (court-83)
items.headline: Supreme Court Directs Inquiry Committee To Examine Journalists' Allegation Of Police Abuse During Delhi CEC Protests
items.claim: The bench of the Chief Justice, Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana on 26 November 2026 sent the petition of the Kerala Union of Working Journalists to the inquiry committee headed by a former judge of the Supreme Court, Justice Subhash Reddy, and asked the committee to examine the allegations of seven Kerala journalists that they were abused by the police and wrongfully detained while covering the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in Delhi in October, and to record its findings of fact, LiveLaw reported. LiveLaw describes the committee as the one the Court constituted in August to inquire into the police action during the student protests of July. The Court asked the journalists to place their material before the committee and disposed of the petition without expressing an opinion on its merits. For the union, the senior advocate P.V. Dinesh said that the Delhi Police had filed a composite counter-affidavit that did not answer the allegations about the seven, and asked for a separate counter-affidavit. He said the journalists claimed no special privilege and asked only to be allowed to do their work. Justice Bagchi said the committee would have to find whether the journalists were present, whether force was used on them and, if so, whether it was more than was needed to keep public order, and the bench said it would examine the wider question of the protection the law gives journalists covering demonstrations. LiveLaw reports that the bench said similar cases of individual journalists could be identified by the nodal counsel and placed before the committee. The petition sought an independent inquiry, action against officials found responsible, compensation for the journalists and guidelines to protect journalists covering public events.
items.quote: Without expressing any opinion on the merits of this case, it is disposed of,
items.response: The Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, said that every allegation had been answered in the counter-affidavit, LiveLaw reported.
